name: Warlpiri
confidence_why: 5 independent first-hand descriptions agree (2 state the same rule, 2 refine it). One further first-hand description conflicts (see the conflicting-description item); the entry follows Berry 1998 1998.
catalog_quote: In an intonation phrase only one main stress is heard in an utterance of one or many words. ... When a word is combined into a sentence, there may be no primary stress on its initial syllable depending on its position in the sentence.
sweep_summary: Warlpiri is in the catalog as fixed-strict (stress placement coded per word length as 10 100 1010 10100 (1 = a stressed syllable), binary+lapse, morpheme-cyclic; deciding quote from Berry 1998:108-109, banked with Poser 1989:142). Four works with stress in the title: (1) Pentland & Laughren 2004 (ALS 2004, held by the project, read): PWd = stress domain, one per polymoraic morpheme, initial stress with finals weak as in Nash 1986; acoustically the stressed syllable is not longer - the cue is post-tonic consonant lengthening, present only utterance-initially; refines (no conflict). (2) Pensalfini 1999 (ALS 1999): NEWLY downloaded sources open from the ALS proceedings site (Glottolog's UWA URL is dead; UQ eSpace copy is captcha-gated); explicit rule - first syllable and every second thereafter, never final; disyllabic suffixes always stressed initially; monosyllabic suffix stressed only when followed by another; root-final odd syllable takes stress before a lone monosyllabic suffix to avoid a lapse; refines/confirms; not previously in our bibliography. (3) Pentland 2004 UQ PhD thesis: record and abstract obtained via the UQ eSpace API (file 'Not Open Access', 403) - instrumental duration study, post-tonic lengthening as a phrase-level cue; silent on placement in the abstract; HIGH priority to acquire (only dedicated first-hand instrumental study, 243 pp.). (4) Abbie 1957 Oceania: anthropometry (Crossref reference list), not relevant. Extra: Butcher & Harrington 2003 ICPhS (held by the project, read) states initial/odd-syllable secondaries/no morpheme-final stress and focus-by-word-order; confirms. Nothing read contradicts the catalog's classification; the deciding source is not superseded (Pensalfini's data are Nash 1980 + Hale/Laughren p.c., the same lineage as Berry/Poser). the Internet Archive was offline

new_statements.quote: The five languages can be characterised in the same way with respect to stress on monomorphemic words: stress falls on the first syllable and on every second syllable thereafter, but never on the final syllable (the distinction between primary and secondary stress is ignored). ... Warlpiri, illustrated in (4), allows a foot to contain nuclei from different morphemes only if a run of three unstressed syllables would otherwise result. Disyllabic suffixes are always stressed on their first syllable. Monosyllabic suffixes are stressed only if followed by another monosyllabic suffix.
new_statements.citation: Pensalfini, Rob (1999/2000). Suffix coherence and stress in Australian languages. Proceedings of the 1999 Conference of the Australian Linguistic Society, pp. 1 and 3 (§2, §2.4); summary rule p. 14.
new_statements.locator: §2 p. 1 (general statement for Pintupi, Diyari, Dyirbal, Warlpiri, Jingulu) and §2.4 Warlpiri p. 3 with data (4a-h); Warlpiri data from Nash 1980 and Hale & Laughren p.c.
new_statements.reading: Word stress in Warlpiri is fixed: initial syllable, then every second syllable, never the word-final syllable, no adjacent stresses - exactly the catalog's 10/100/1010/10100.. profile (binary+lapse) - and the count restarts on every polysyllabic morpheme (catalog's morpheme-cyclic flag). It adds one refinement the catalog quote does not state: to avoid three unstressed syllables in a row, the final syllable of an odd-syllable root takes secondary stress when followed by exactly one monosyllabic suffix ((wáti)(yà-rla)), whereas two monosyllabic suffixes foot together ((wáti)ya-(rlà-rlu)). Butcher & Harrington 2003 p.1 and Pentland & Laughren 2004 §3.1/§7 (both read) agree on initial/alternating/non-final and per-morpheme domains.

new_statements.second_reader_bearing_note: confirms the catalog's classification (fixed-strict, initial + alternating non-final, binary+lapse, word domain, morphology-sensitive), but as a secondary/comparative synthesis of Nash 1980 + Hale/Laughren p.c., not a first-hand statement; it does not distinguish primary from secondary stress and says nothing about phrase-level stress, so it cannot replace Nash 1980:100 / Berry 1998:26 (positions + initial primary) or Berry 1998:108-109 (domain) as the deciding sources.

tone_statements.citation: Babinski, Sarah. 2026. Stress in Australian languages: A phonetic typology. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 56(e5): 1-28. doi:10.1017/S0025100325100832
tone_statements.quote: Pitch (f0) peaks are very commonly correlated with stress, as Figure 5 shows. An increase of 1 semitone in stressed vowels corresponds to an increase in f0 of about 6%; most languages in this study have effects around this size, with the exception of Wanyjirra and Warnman, which have relatively more variable, and non-significant, results here. [p.11] ... It seems, based on relative effect sizes, that f0 is the strongest cue to stress in these languages, or at least that high f0 is a stronger cue than lengthened vowels [...] While this study controlled for some common phrasal effects in its modeling by adjusting for initial, medial, and final phrasal positions, it did not address the question of whether word-initial f0 peaks are indeed cues to lexical stress rather than an edge-marking prosodic phenomenon that operates on the word level. [p.18; Table 3 p.18, Warlpiri column: Intensity yes / F0 maximum yes / F0 range no / Vowel duration yes]

tone_statements.summary: No lexical tone; f0 peak on the initial (stressed) syllable = stress/edge correlate (post-lexical).

tone_statements.citation: Chapman, Jeff (2007). Intonational marking of focus in Warlpiri narratives. Abstract, OzPhon07: Workshop on the Phonetics and Phonology of Australian Languages, La Trobe University, Melbourne, 3-4 December 2007; abstracts booklet p. 7.
tone_statements.quote: Butcher and Harrington (2003) reported on focus in Warlpiri sentences, and showed that phrase initial focused elements had a pitch accent which does not occur in postverbal elements, which are not in focus. To further investigate the relationship between intonation and information structure in Warlpiri, this study analysed recordings of three narrative texts, from three different Warlpiri speakers. The analysis of these texts confirms that intonation is related to the information structure, and that a higher initial intonation can be found on words that contain relatively new information (rheme rather than theme) . This higher intonation does not seem to be directly related to word order or to those aspects of focus which contribute to 'prominence'. Moreover, the intonational prominence found on new information is relatively small compared to the changes in fundamental frequency associated with pitch accents found in a language such as English, raising questions about the phonological status of the change in intonation found in Warlpiri.
tone_statements.summary: No lexical tone; small utterance-/word-initial F0 raising on new information; phonological pitch accent status doubtful.

tone_statements.citation: Chapman, Jeffrey (2007). Some Aspects of Intonation in Warlpiri. Paper and abstract, Workshop on Australian Languages, Pearl Beach (University of Sydney), 16-18 March 2007; abstract in the online workshop program (J. Simpson, comp.).
tone_statements.quote: The recordings were annotated in an autosegmental-metrical framework using a tones and break indices (ToBI) style notation. The principal findings which I will discuss were: - Many words conformed to a standard intonation contour, with a high initial tone and a gradual fall in intonation to a low final tone. - Verb compounds and the auxiliary complex show a single falling contour, leading to the conclusion that these expressions are a single accentual phrase (Beckman and Pierrehumbert, 1986), bounded by initial high and final low tones. - No evidence was found for a culminative accent on words with either narrow or broad focus. Warlpiri uses a final rising intonation in questions, and final lowering at the end of a number of declarative utterances.
tone_statements.locator: program page, abstracts section, entry 'Jeff Chapman, University of Queensland Australia - Some Aspects of Intonation in Warlpiri' (bullet list of principal findings)
tone_statements.summary: No lexical tone; accentual phrases with initial H and final L edge tones; no culminative pitch accent.

tone_statements.citation: King, Heather B. (1999). High onset pitch accents? The case of Dyirbal and Warlpiri. In Proceedings of the 14th International Congress of Phonetic Sciences (ICPhS-99), San Francisco, 1-7 August 1999, pp. 2403-2406.
tone_statements.quote: Both Dyirbal and Warlpiri employ an increase in pitch to indicate accentuation. In both languages a pitch accent occurs on the first syllable of an accented word. … 2.2.2. Warlpiri. Intonation in Warlpiri is phrasal rather than focal. Each syntactic phrase has an accent on the first word unless, under pragmatic constraints, the phrase is deaccented (i.e., dephrased) and is included in the domain of the accent of the previous phrase [5].
tone_statements.summary: No lexical tone; pitch is intonational: high pitch accents (rising H* 'A1', possibly a distinct high-onset 'A2') dock on the initial stressed syllable of the first word of each syntactic phrase, with pragmatic deaccenting/dephrasing.

sources.citation: Pentland, Christina & Laughren, Mary (2004). Distinguishing prosodic word and phonological word in Warlpiri: prosodic constituency in morphologically complex words. Proceedings of the 2004 Conference of the Australian Linguistic Society, 17 pp.
sources.quote: In Nash's model, the phonological word is the stress domain. Morphologically complex words such as compounds and reduplications are analysed as phonological words containing two or more prosodic words (or domains). ... The model predicts that the primary stress of the verb kuju-rnu is demoted to secondary stress in the compound structure ... We therefore propose that a model of Warlpiri prosody must recognize two word-level constituents: the prosodic word (PWd), which is the stress domain, and the phonological word (PhonWd), which is the domain of regressive vowel harmony and case allomorphy rules.

sources.note: Does not restate the placement rule in prose; it takes Nash 1986's analysis as given (each prosodic word = a stress domain with initial stress, finals weak, as in tree (3) pirri[s w] kujurnu[s w w]) and argues that every polymoraic morpheme (root, preverb, disyllabic suffix) is its own PWd/stress domain even inside a single phonological word - i.e. stress restarts per morpheme. sources.note: Pitch in Warlpiri is treated only as an acoustic correlate of fixed word-initial stress, not as lexical tone: in the Warlpiri sub-corpus (one speaker) stressed vowels have a significantly higher f0 maximum (+1.03 semitones, Table B8; 'F0 maximum: yes' in Table 3) but no difference in f0 range ('F0 range: no'), alongside higher intensity (+3.98 dB, the largest in the sample) and longer vowels; across the 13 languages a high f0 peak is the commonest and strongest stress cue, and the author leaves open whether these word-initial f0 peaks cue lexical stress or are word-edge boundary marking.

sources.citation: Butcher, Andrew & Jonathan Harrington. 2003. An instrumental analysis of focus and juncture in Warlpiri. In M.J. Solé, D. Recasens & J. Romero (eds.), Proceedings of the 15th International Congress of Phonetic Sciences, Barcelona, 321-324.
sources.quote: 'There is general agreement that "stress" in Warlpiri is fixed on morpheme-initial syllables and that there may be "secondary stresses" on every other subsequent odd-numbered syllable, with the exception that morpheme-final syllables are not stressed (e.g., /mánaŋkàra/, "spinifex plain", [11]).'
sources.note: Summary by the phoneticians running the instrumental work: primary stress fixed on morpheme-initial syllables, secondary on subsequent odd-numbered syllables, morpheme-final syllables never stressed; focus is signalled by word order (phrase-initial position), not by shifting stress. Confirms the catalog row (initial, alternating, never final, morpheme-cyclic).

Each syntactic phrase has an accent on the first word unless, under pragmatic constraints, the phrase is deaccented (i.e., dephrased) and is included in the domain of the accent of the previous phrase [5].
tone.summary: No lexical tone; pitch is intonational: high pitch accents (rising H* 'A1', possibly a distinct high-onset 'A2') dock on the initial stressed syllable of the first word of each syntactic phrase, with pragmatic deaccenting/dephrasing.
tone.says: No lexical tone described: pitch is intonational, a high pitch accent on the first (stressed) syllable of the first word of each phrase; two phonetic shapes of the high accent (rising, high-onset).

tone.quote: The impressionistic description of the correlates of stress made by Nash are: increased intensity, increased duration, and higher pitch. ... Using f0 to mark consistent initial stress may function not just as a stress correlate, but also as a prosodic marker of phonological word and phrase boundaries. ... Yidiny, Yan­nhangu, and Warlpiri all have correlations predicting stressed syllables to have f0 values about 1 semitone higher than unstressed ones.

sources.quote: The first result confirms previous findings that consonants following primary stressed syllables are lengthened. This process, which is sometimes called post-tonic lengthening, is considered a s[t]ress cue in several Australian languages. However, the findings in this thesis suggest instead [that] post-tonic lengthening in Warlpiri, which only affects post-tonic consonants in words that are also utterance-initial, might be a higher-level prosodic cue associated with phrasal or utterance-level prominence. The second result indicates that consonant duration (i.e., lengthening) is also used as a cue to signal word boundaries and some morpheme bo[u]ndaries.
sources.note: The only instrumental monograph on Warlpiri word stress (duration/strengthening correlates, stress domains); our record rests on impressionistic descriptions (Nash, Berry) and would gain an acoustic check of initial prominence and of the secondary-stress pattern.
